\section{Literature And Novelty Boundary}
The related-work function is to separate target formulation, standard machinery, closest comparators, and novelty boundaries.
\begin{itemize}
\item 1971-1972: Verification becomes a universal computational phenomenon: Cook and Karp show that many apparently different problems are interreducible through polynomial reductions and share SAT as a complete core. What remained open: Completeness explains universality of difficulty but not the source of lower bounds against all polynomial-time algorithms or circuits.
\item 1975: Proof techniques become objects of study: Relativization shows that any proof surviving arbitrary oracle substitution cannot settle the main question. What remained open: The barrier diagnoses broad method families but does not identify a successful nonrelativizing replacement.
\item Late 1970s onward: Complexity becomes a landscape of representations: Algebraic, proof-complexity, descriptive, and structural viewpoints re-express computation through polynomials, proofs, reductions, and uniformity conditions. What remained open: Every translation risks losing target strength: a theorem in a restricted or algebraic model must still return to Boolean P vs NP or P/poly with controlled loss.
\item 1990s: Lower-bound intuitions meet pseudorandomness: Natural proofs explain why many broad, efficiently checkable combinatorial properties are unlikely to prove strong unrestricted circuit lower bounds. What remained open: The field still needs useful lower-bound properties that are either not large, not constructive, not black-box, or otherwise outside the natural-proofs template.
\item 2000s onward: Fine-grained and magnification thinking exposes exponent debt: Hardness transfers are judged by exact exponents, target-query counts, advice leakage, and whether a weak source lower bound really magnifies to the main target. What remained open: Most bridges lose too much exponent, import nonuniform advice, or prove a source lower bound that is already as hard as the desired conclusion.
\item 2009 onward: Modern progress is real but carefully scoped: Algebrization and restricted-circuit lower bounds clarify both the reach and limits of current techniques. What remained open: The unrestricted P vs NP question still demands a target-preserving lower bound or impossibility theorem that escapes known barriers without losing the main quantifiers.
\item ref.cook-1971: The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures. Supports: Introduces NP-completeness through satisfiability and turns efficient verification into a universal problem.. Limitation: It defines the central complete problem and reduction method; it does not separate deterministic from nondeterministic polynomial time.
\item ref.karp-1972: Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems. Supports: Shows that many natural search and optimization problems share the same NP-complete core.. Limitation: NP-completeness transfers difficulty conditionally; it does not prove that any NP-complete problem lacks polynomial algorithms.
\end{itemize}

\section{Route Narrowing And Scientific Learning}
The route history is included only where it explains why the paper object became narrower and more testable.
\begin{itemize}
\item cycle-0002: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: Cycle 2 turns the previous threshold collapse into an exact quantifier repair. The valid route lemma is: fixed k gives only a finite SAT exponent lower bound, while a common-epsilon lower bound for unbounded padded carriers H\_k would imply NP not subset P/poly. The decisive falsifier is not folklore but the inequality c/k>=1+epsilon, plus the O(N) checker floor.
\item cycle-0003: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: Cycle 3 finds a valid single-carrier repair: growth padding N\_m=(m+1)\textasciicircum{}\{g(m+1)\} converts an i.o. N\textasciicircum{}\{1+epsilon\} lower bound for H\_g into exclusion of every SAT exponent c. This is route-level progress, not P vs NP; the hard obligation is now the sparse valid-length lower bound.
\item cycle-0004: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: Cycle 4 proves a valid projection-sandwich lemma and demagnifies the sparse-padding route: N\textasciicircum{}\{1+eps\} lower bounds for H\_g equal m\textasciicircum{}\{(1+eps)g\} SAT lower bounds. The bridge is correct but not a weak-source path toward P vs NP.
\item cycle-0006: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization, Cycle 6: MCSP verifier transfer audit: Cycle 6 shows that moving from projection padding to a nonprojection MCSP carrier does not by itself create major magnification. The valid transfer is C(MCSP\_\{N\textasciicircum{}alpha\},N)<=N\textasciicircum{}\{c(1+alpha)+o(1)\} under SAT in SIZE(n\textasciicircum{}c), so an N\textasciicircum{}\{1+epsilon\} source lower bound excludes only c<(1+epsilon)/(1+alpha). The input-reading floor alpha>=0 caps any fixed barely-superlinear bridge below all-exponent P/poly separation. The failure is a concrete threshold falsifier, not barrier folklore.
\item cycle-0009: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: subpolynomial-interface demagnification: Cycle 9 converts the cycle-8 repair into a route failure certificate. Subpolynomial SAT queries remove the c-dependent upper-bound term, but the same transfer read backward says that proving the source N\textasciicircum{}\{1+epsilon\} lower bound in general SIZE already proves SAT\_\{<=L\} has L\textasciicircum{}\{omega(1)\} circuits lower bounds. The remaining valid work is not carrier search inside this black-box same-model interface; it is either a restricted-model closure theorem or a nonblackbox carrier.
\item cycle-0010: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: Cycle 10 proves a valid restricted-model closure bridge and names the precise target-preservation failure. Subpolynomial queries plus max(a,q)<1+epsilon magnify a Gamma lower bound to SAT notin Gamma/poly for every fixed exponent. This is real route-level progress, but it is not NP notin P/poly: the missing object is a nonuniform P/poly-to-Gamma lift with subthreshold tax, and its absence is the decisive falsifier for advertising the bridge as a P vs NP route.
\item cycle-0012: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: Cycle 12 identifies a real surviving window: superlogarithmic subpolynomial target lengths, especially L=(log N)\textasciicircum{}d with d>1. In this window SAT circuits of size L\textasciicircum{}c amortize to N\textasciicircum{}\{o(1)\}, but SAT truth tables cost 2\textasciicircum{}L and no longer give the old subthreshold lookup falsifier. The bridge is valid only for nonblackbox compact-circuit consumers; it is not a P vs NP proof without the explicit carrier and lower bound.
\item cycle-0013: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: Polylog Nonblackbox Compact Consumer: Cycle 13 turns the superlogarithmic polylog window into an exact bridge: L=(log N)\textasciicircum{}d with d>1 makes SAT circuits of size L\textasciicircum{}c amortize to N\textasciicircum{}\{o(1)\}, while truth-table lookup costs 2\textasciicircum{}L=N\textasciicircum{}\{omega(1)\} and no longer supplies the old falsifier. The valid threshold is rho<1+epsilon for a target-clean nonblackbox compact consumer. The new hard obstruction is not folklore but the absence of an explicit carrier with no advice leakage and a non-natural N\textasciicircum{}\{1+epsilon\} general-circuit lower bound.
\end{itemize}

\section{Worked Calculation And Falsifier Tests}
The worked-calculation section records what is computable now and what exact transfer, threshold, falsifier, or remainder test would decide promotion or demotion.
\begin{itemize}
\item cycle-0004: threshold\_demagnification
\[
C_{N_m}(H_g)> N_m^{1+\epsilon}\Rightarrow C_m(SAT)> (m+1)^{(1+\epsilon)g(m+1)}-O(m)
\]
\item cycle-0005: Hardness-Magnification Bridge Realization: Cycle 5 converts the padding quarantine into a general projection-carrier dichotomy. The valid bridge says N\textasciicircum{}\{1+epsilon\} lower bounds transfer through ell(N) only when ell(N)\textasciicircum{}c is below the threshold. Positive polynomial embedding length gives only a bounded exponent window; subpolynomial embedding length gives all exponents but turns the source lower bound into ell(N)\textasciicircum{}\{omega(1)\}. Thus pure projection magnification fails as a weak-source path, with an explicit falsifier rather than a slogan.
\item cycle-0005: projection\_upper\_bound
\[
\mathrm{SIZE}(H_N) \le A N+B\,\mathrm{SIZE}(\mathrm{SAT}_{\ell(N)})+O(N\log N).
\]
\item cycle-0005: exponent\_transfer
\[
\mathrm{SIZE}(\mathrm{SAT}_m)\le m^c\ \forall m \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathrm{SIZE}(H_N)\le O(N\log N)+\ell(N)^c.
\]
\item cycle-0005: finite\_window
\[
\ell(N)=N^{\alpha+o(1)}\ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{SIZE}(H_N)\le N^{\alpha c+o(1)}+O(N\log N).
\]
\item cycle-0005: contradiction\_condition
\[
K N^{1+\varepsilon}< \mathrm{SIZE}(H_N)\ \mathrm{i.o.}\ \wedge\ \alpha c< 1+\varepsilon\ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{SAT}\notin \mathrm{SIZE}(n^c).
\]
\item cycle-0005: all\_exponents\_cost
\[
(\forall c\;\ell(N)^c=o(N^{1+\varepsilon}))\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \ell(N)=N^{o(1)},\quad \ell(N)=N^{o(1)}\Rightarrow N^{1+\varepsilon}=\ell(N)^{\omega(1)}.
\]
\item cycle-0006: verifier\_time
\[
T_\alpha(N)=O(N\,s(N)\,\mathrm{polylog}\,N)=N^{1+\alpha+o(1)}
\]
\item cycle-0006: induced\_upper\_bound
\[
\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{SIZE}(m^c)\Rightarrow C(K_{\alpha,N})\le N^{c(1+\alpha)+o(1)}
\]
\item cycle-0006: transfer\_threshold
\[
C(K_{\alpha,N})> N^{1+\epsilon}\Rightarrow \mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{SIZE}(n^c)\quad\text{for }c< \frac{1+\epsilon}{1+\alpha}
\]
\end{itemize}
